replies:
Great — I'll mock you for a financial analyst interview.

First question (answer as you would in the room; I'll score it and give one concrete improvement, then ask the next):

"Walk me through a financial model you've built: what was the business question, what inputs and assumptions did you use, how did you structure the model, what was the result, and how did stakeholders use it?"

Score: 2/10.

Quick, concrete rewrite using STAR and a result metric (I filled numbers as placeholders you must replace with real ones from your experience):
"Situation: At [Company], the finance team needed a consolidated forecast to decide whether to fund a new product line. Task: I had to build a three-statement model that tested pricing and volume scenarios and produced cash flow and ROI estimates for the CFO. Action: I built the model in [your skill], driving revenue from unit volumes, price, and mix; linked COGS, operating expenses and working capital schedules; and added a dynamic scenario tab with toggles for price, volume and gross margin. I cross-checked implied margins and valuation multiples against three public comps and automated key outputs with formulas and pivot summaries. Result: The model showed the base-case return on invested
capital improved by 18% under the approved pricing, reducing forecast variance by ~25% versus the prior model; the CFO used it to approve the project and set a $[X] budget."

Now your turn: replace the bracketed items with your real facts — company, tool (Excel or Python), the number of comps, the exact result metric(s) and any budget or decision that followed. Give one concrete metric for Result (%, $ or time saved). Which real example do you want me to score next?

Honest score: 2/10.

Why: Your answer names the right high-level steps (three-statement model, revenue drivers, comps) but it misses what interviewers listen for:
- Situation: where and why you built the model (what decision or problem).
- Task: your specific responsibility or target (what you were asked to deliver).
- Actions: concrete steps, tools and mechanics (what inputs, schedules, formulas, validations you actually built).
- Result: a concrete outcome with numbers (impact on a decision, $ saved, % improvement, faster process).
What to fix (one-step checklist):
1) Add the brief Situation and Task (one sentence total).
2) Replace vague Actions with 3 specific mechanics you did (e.g., "built monthly revenue drivers by SKU linked to a DCF, created a working-capital schedule tied to AR days, automated scenario toggles with data validation and INDEX-MATCH").
3) Give one measurable Result (%, $, or time) and the decision or action that followed.
4) Say the tool you used ([your skill], SQL, Python) and the number of comps you checked.
Improved two-sentence version you can use immediately (fill with your facts):
"At [Company], I built a three-statement model to decide whether to fund a new product line; I was asked to produce scenario returns and a cash-flow forecast for the CFO. I modeled revenue from unit volume, price and mix in Excel, linked COGS and a working-cap schedule, added scenario toggles and stress tests, and validated margins against three comps — the model showed a [X]% IRR and led leadership to approve a $[Y] allocation."

Want me to score a filled-in version if you paste one with your real numbers and company?

You don't have any Lincoln International interviews or prep materials on file yet. The one step that starts that: paste the interview invite (or tell me the date/time, who you'll meet, and whether it's case/fit/technical) so I can tailor the briefing and questions to the exact round.

Below is a focused final-round prep you can use now. I assumed this is for an Analyst role in investment banking / M&A (Lincoln International's common track), and the final round will include behavioral/fit questions, technical finance/accounting questions, and one or two brief case or modeling tasks. If any of that is off, say which and I'll adjust.
1) What they want to hear (one sentence)
- Clear evidence you understand basic deal mechanics, you can handle modeling and diligence tasks accurately and quickly, you work well on small teams, and you’re motivated for client-facing M&A work.
2) Top 8 likely question types and how to answer them (short script + what to include)
- "Walk me through your resume."
- 60–90s: present, most relevant experience first, one line on results for each role (what you did, the impact with a number), end with "why Lincoln" link: team/firm fit + recent deal or sector interest.
- "Why Lincoln International / why M&A advisory?"
- One crisp reason tied to the firm (mid-market focus, deal exposure, culture) + two examples: 1) what you liked about a Lincoln deal or team, 2) how your background preps you to add value.
- "Tell me about a time you worked on a team under tight deadline."
- Use STAR: Situation (short), Task (your responsibility), Action (concrete steps you took — prioritize, delegate, quality checks), Result (quantified if possible). Highlight communication and accuracy under pressure.
- Technical: "Walk me through an LBO / DCF / three-statement link" (pick the ones they use in interviews)
- Short structure: purpose, steps, key drivers, sensitivities. For DCF: project FCF -> discount at WACC -> terminal value (gordon or exit) -> enterprise value -> equity value. Mention key sensitivities: revenue growth, margins, capex, working capital, discount rate.
- Accounting: "How does an increase in inventory affect the three statements?"
- Income: no immediate effect on P&L (COGS timing) — unless write-down; Cash Flow: increase in inventory uses cash in operating CF (working capital increase); Balance Sheet: inventory up (asset) and cash down; net effect on equity same unless margin change. Tie back to timing and working capital cycle.
- Valuation/comps: "How would you value X company?"
- Start: choose methods (comps, precedent transactions, DCF). List 3–4 comps selection criteria (size, margin, growth, geography). Explain multiples you'd use and key adjustments (non-recurring items, leases, minority interests).
- Fit: "What’s a weakness / failure?"
- Short honest failure, emphasize learning and the concrete change you made. Avoid cliché “too hard-working”; show self-awareness and improvement.
- Case/Modeling task: "Here’s a short case — estimate EBITDA / value this business"
- Walk through assumptions out loud: revenue drivers, margin progression, capex as % of revenue, working capital days. Show rough math, highlight that assumptions drive output and show sensitivity.
3) Quick one-minute answers to practice (templates)
- "Why you?"
  - "I bring X months/years of [relevant experience: modeling, financial analysis, transaction support], proven accuracy under tight deadlines (example: [task and result]), and a clear interest in [sector]; I want to join Lincoln because of its mid-market focus and the hands-on exposure it offers to deal execution."
- "Where do you see yourself in 3–5 years?"
  - "Contributing as a trusted analyst on execution teams, owning due diligence and model work, and progressing to associate-level responsibilities while developing a sector specialty in [sector]."
4) Technical brush-up checklist (what to review in 24–48 hours)
- LBO and DCF step-by-step calculations (free cash flow, terminal value methods, WACC inputs).
- Three-statement tying and common journal entries (depreciation, deferred tax, debt issuance).
- Working capital math (days sales outstanding, days payable outstanding, days inventory outstanding).
- Common M&A adjustments (EBITDA add-backs, normalizing working capital, treatment of leases).
- Recent Lincoln International deals (2–3; read the announcement and one short note on value drivers).
5) Case strategy (if you get a short take-home or whiteboard case)
- Clarify objective and timeline first.
- State your structure: 1) revenue drivers & growth, 2) margins & cost structure, 3) capex and working capital, 4) high-level valuation methods, 5) sensitivities.
- Keep numbers rounded (e.g., 10s/100s) and show calculation steps. Always state assumptions.
- Finish with recommendation and two risks/mitigants.

6) Behavioral answers — scoring checklist I’ll use when I score your practice answers
- Situation present? Action you took? Metrics/result? Relevance to role?  (Aim to hit all 4)
7) 10-point final-round prep plan (what to do in the 48 hours before)
- Re-read the job description and any senior bankers’ bios.
- Review any interviewers’ LinkedIn profiles (roles, deal history).
- Refresh DCF/LBO and one small worked example.
- Prepare 6 STAR stories: leadership, teamwork, failure, conflict, handle ambiguity, delivering under pressure.
- Read 2–3 Lincoln deal press releases and note one insight about each.
- Prepare 3 questions to ask them (team workload, recent deal, training/mentoring).
- Mock 30–45 minute interview with me or a peer; practice concise storytelling.
- Sleep, plan travel / logistics, print one-page cheat sheet with bullet points.
- Ready your market-rate and notice-period answers (if asked).
- Have closing line: why you, and your enthusiasm for the firm’s model.

8) Closing-line scripts to use if asked for final pitch
- "I want this role because the mid-market, hands-on deal work suits how I learn and add value; my recent [experience] gives me the modeling rigor, and I thrive in the fast, small-team environment Lincoln is known for."

Next step: paste the interview invite (or tell me the date/time, who you'll meet, and whether it’s a case/model or mostly fit/behavioral). I’ll make a targeted 1-page brief and 8 practice questions tailored to the exact interviewers and format. Is that the invite you can paste now?
